blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string `s`, you may add letters **in front of it** only. Return the shortest palindrome you can make this way.

blocks.alt: s equals aacecaaa. Its first seven letters, aacecaa, already form a palindrome; only the last letter, a, is left over. Adding that leftover, reversed, to the front gives aaacecaaa, the shortest answer. Below, the KMP way to find that prefix: the string s, a hash sign, then s reversed. The longest prefix of this combined string that is also a suffix is aacecaa, seven letters, which is exactly the palindrome at the start of s.

elements.text: keep the longest palindrome at the start; mirror the rest in front

elements.text: t = s + "#" + reverse(s): its longest border is that palindrome

elements.text: lps of t ends in 7: keep 7 letters, add 8 - 7 = 1

blocks.code:
s = "aacecaaa"  ->  "aaacecaaa"   (keep "aacecaa", add "a")
s = "abcd"      ->  "dcbabcd"     (keep "a", add "dcb")
s = "racecar"   ->  "racecar"     (already a palindrome)

blocks.text: The idea: the longest palindrome at the start

Whatever is added in front must mirror the end of `s`. So the best you can do is keep the longest **prefix of s that is already a palindrome** as the middle, and put the rest of `s`, reversed, in front. For `"abcd"` the longest palindrome prefix is just `"a"`, so `"dcb"` goes in front: `"dcbabcd"`.

Finding that prefix is the whole problem. Testing each prefix from longest to shortest is O(n²). KMP finds it in O(n) with one trick: a palindrome prefix `P` read backwards is still `P`, and it sits at the **end of reverse(s)**. So `P` is a **border** of `s + "#" + reverse(s)` — a prefix that is also a suffix — and the KMP table's last entry gives the longest one. The `#` can't match any letter, so no border can be longer than `s`.
**Time O(n²), space O(n).** Up to n prefixes, each checked in up to n / 2 comparisons. Inputs like `"aaaa…aaba…aaaa"` hit the worst case: every check runs deep before failing.

blocks.caption: Build the KMP table for s # reverse(s); its last entry is the longest palindrome at the start of s.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** One KMP table over 2n + 1 letters, then one slice. Why it's right: a border of length L has `s[0..L)` at the front of `t` and `reverse(s[0..L))` at the back, so equal means `s[0..L)` is a palindrome — and the longest border is the longest such prefix.

rows.timeWhy: Up to **n** prefixes, each checked in up to **n/2** comparisons.
One **KMP table** over 2n + 1 letters, then one slice.

blocks.text: This is the hardest lesson in the pattern because the reduction is the whole trick: once the question becomes *longest border of s # reverse(s)*, KMP does the rest.

items: **No long palindrome prefix** — `"abcd"` keeps only `"a"` and becomes `"dcbabcd"`.
**Leaving out the `#`** — for `"aaa"`, `s + reverse(s)` is `"aaaaaa"`, whose border is 5 letters: longer than `s`, and the slice breaks.
**Longest Palindromic Substring** — expanding around the centre (Pattern 6), or Manacher's algorithm for O(n).
**Longest Happy Prefix** — return the longest border of a string: exactly `lps[n - 1]`.
**Palindrome Pairs** — which pairs of words join into a palindrome? It uses the same split: a palindrome part plus a reversed rest that must exist in the word list.
